To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the protein sparing effect of a parenteral nutrition is mainly dependent on the rate of amino acids supply.

(1) the protein sparing effect of amino acids supplementation depends on the dose and the composition of the mixture; (2) the protein sparing effects are not influenced by the energy supply; (3) fat emulsions can be used for calorie supply in the postoperative course; (4) the use of special amino acids mixt...

1) adequate amino acids supply is the dominating protein sparing factor, 2) low calorie supply is of comparable protein sparing benefit, 3) fat emulsions are of metabolic advantage compared with an exclusive and high calorie glucose supply and 4) amino acids supply has to be adapted to the trauma induced changes in amino acids metabolism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question, how the different protein-sparing effects of the single nutritional components can be used for the best clinical benefit.
the question of the optimal amino acid composition of parenteral nutritional regimens.
the question of the influence of the composition of amino acids mixtures and the rate of supply on protein-sparing mechanisms in the clinical situation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
parenteral feeding should always be adapted to the individual metabolic situation of each patient.

in clinical situations of high protein losses, the use of amino acids solutions is of primary importance, whereas the influence of calorie supply and special amino acids mixture is limited and not clearly defined yet.
in acute catabolic conditions a high-dosed, balanced amino acid supply represents the dominating protein-sparing mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the protein sparing effect of parenteral feeding is mainly determined by the adequate supply with essential amino acids, but that the additional supply of non-protein substrates--carbohydrate and fat--also has a favourable influence.
parenteral nutrition in acute diseased states has to be adapted to the metabolic situation, i.e. to the degree of acute protein losses.
in the acute diseased state the adequate supply of essential amino acids is the most important factor in protein sparing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
parenteral nutrition should be tailored to individual patient's metabolic needs.
a high-dose amino acid supplementation is the key to the success of parenteral nutrition.
the protein-sparing effect of amino acid substitution is the dominant mechanism during the early phase of trauma and operation.
